bio.en: Simon Willison is a renowned engineer and one of the most useful voices on how AI is changing software and knowledge work; he co-created Django, coined 'prompt injection,' popularized 'AI slop' and 'agentic engineering,' and maintains 100+ open-source projects.
bio.zh: Simon Willison 是一位知名的工程师，也是关于“AI 如何改变软件与知识工作”最具实用价值的声音之一；他共同创造了 Django 框架、提出了“提示注入（prompt injection）”一词、普及了“AI slop”与“智能体工程（agentic engineering）”，并维护着 100 多个开源项目。

summary.en: Simon shares a pragmatic, builder's view of the AI shift, emphasizing that the real unlock is using LLMs as tools in your own workflow rather than waiting for magic. He discusses local and open models, the rise of AI agents, and why data and UX still decide whether an AI product actually works. The conversation is grounded, skeptical in the best way, and full of concrete habits for engineers and knowledge workers.
summary.zh: Simon 分享了对 AI 变革的、务实的“构建者视角”，强调真正的突破口是把大语言模型当作自己工作流中的工具来用，而非坐等魔法降临。他讨论了本地与开源模型、AI 智能体的兴起，以及为何数据与用户体验仍决定一款 AI 产品是否真的好用。对话立足现实、以最佳方式保持怀疑，并充满了面向工程师与知识工作者的具体习惯。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: A lot of people woke up in January and February and started realizing, "Oh wow, I can churn out 10,000 lines of code in a day." It used to be you'd ask ChatGPT for some code and it would spit out some code, and you have to run it and test it. The coding agents, they take that step for you, and an open question for me is how many other knowledge work fields are actually prone to these agent loops?
turns.zh: 一开年的一二月，很多人突然意识到："哇，我一天能哗哗写出一万行代码。"以前你找 ChatGPT 要段代码，它吐给你一段，你还得自己跑、自己测。而现在的编程智能体（coding agents）帮你把这一步也做了。我一直在想一个悬而未决的问题：还有多少知识工作领域，其实也适合这种智能体循环？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now that we have this power, people almost underestimate what they do with it.
turns.zh: 现在我们有了这股力量，但人们几乎低估了能用它做成的事。

turns.en: Today probably 95% of the code that I produce I didn't type it myself. I write so much of my code on my phone, it's wild. I can get good work done walking the dog along the beach. This year my ambition was take on more stuff and be more ambitious.

turns.speaker: Simon Willison

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Well, let's talk about all of 2025 very briefly. 2025 was the year that especially Anthropic and OpenAI realized that code is the application, like having these things generate code. I think partly because Anthropic came up with Claude Code back in February of 2025, and it took off like crazy, and a bunch of people started signing up for $200 a month accounts. So, suddenly, wow, it turns out people are willing to pay a lot of money for this stuff for that specific field. Both Anthropic and OpenAI spent the whole of 2025 focusing all of their training efforts on coding. If you look at what they were doing, it was all the reinforcement learning stuff. The reasoning trick, the thing where the models say they're thinking, that was new in late 2024. OpenAI's o1 was the first model to exhibit that, and now all of the models do it. So, that was the other big trend of last year was these reasoning models. (00:04:23): Turns out reasoning is great for code. It can reason through code and figure out the root of bugs and all of that. So the end result of this, the end result of these two labs throwing everything they had at making their models better at code is in November we had what I call the inflection point where GPT 5.1 and Claude Opus 4.5 came along. They were incrementally better than the previous models, but in a way that crossed a threshold, where previously if you had these coding agents you could get them to write you some code and most of the time it would mostly work, but you had to pay very close attention to it. Suddenly we went from that to almost all of the time it does what you told it to do, which makes all of the difference in the world. (00:05:04): Now, you can spin up a coding agent and say, "Hey, build me a Mac application that does this thing." You'll get something back, which still leads some back and forth, but it won't just be a buggy pile of rubbish that doesn't do anything. That was fascinating, because all of the software engineers who took time off over the holidays and started tinkering with this stuff got this moment of realization where it's like, "Oh, wow, this stuff actually works now. I could tell it to build code, and if I describe that code well enough, it'll follow the instructions and it'll build the thing that I asked it to build." (00:05:33): I think the reverberations of that are still shaking us. To software engineering, a lot of people woke up in January and February and started realizing, "Oh wow, this technology, which I'd been kind of paying attention to, suddenly it's got really, really good." And what does that mean? I can churn out 10,000 lines of code in a day and most of it works. Is that good? How do we get from most of it works to all of it works? There are so many new questions that we're facing, which I think makes us a bellwether for other information workers. (00:06:04): Code is easier than almost every other problem that you pose these agents, because code is obviously right or wrong. It produces code, you run the code, either it works or it doesn't work. There might be a few subtle hidden bugs, but generally you can tell if the thing actually works. If it writes you an essay or if it prepares a lawsuit for you, it's so much harder to derive if it's actually done a good job to figure out if it got things right or wrong, but it's kind of happening to us. (00:06:33): So software engineers, it came for us first and we're figuring out, okay, what do our careers look like? How do we work as teams when part of what we did that used to take look most of the time doesn't take most of the time anymore, what's that look like? It's going to be very interesting seeing how this rolls out to other information work in the future.

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Let's talk about the two, there's the vibe coding side of things and then there's the ... and I like Andrej Karpathy's original definition of vibe coding, which is when you don't even look at code and you basically just go on the vibes. You say, build me something that does X, and it builds it and you play with it. If it looks good, then great, and if it doesn't quite do it, you keep on going back and forth with it. But it's very hands-off, you're not looking at code, it's ... so he originally said, "This is great for having fun and prototyping," and it then exploded way out of that. (00:09:21): I think today vibe coding is effectively it's ... the definition I use is it's when you're not looking at the code, you don't care about code and maybe you don't understand the code. Non-programmers can now tell Claude what to build and it can build them a little app, and I love that. I absolutely love that we're democratizing the art of getting a computer to do stuff for you, of automating tedious things in your life by knocking out these little tools. Of course, the problem is that there is a limit on how much you can do with that responsibly. I like to tell people, if you're vibe coding something for yourself where the only person who gets hurt if it has bugs is you, go wild. That's completely fine. The moment you're vibe coding code for other people to use where your bugs might actually harm somebody else, that's when you need to take a step back and say, hang on a second, this is not a responsible way of using these tools. (00:10:15): The challenge is that understanding what's responsible and what isn't is in itself a expert level skill, so knowing that once you start dealing with scraping other people's websites, maybe you'll damage their websites by hitting them too hard. There are so many ways that you can cause damage if you don't know what you're doing. But I love that liberation and I love that people can come to meetings with a prototype that they knocked up of that idea that illustrates the idea. I think those things are wonderful. (00:10:42): The ongoing debate has been what do we call it when a professional software engineer uses these tools to write real code that's production-ready that they've reviewed and they've checked all of the details of? A lot of people call that vibe coding as well. I think that devalues vibe coding as a term, 'cause it's useful to say, "I vibe coded this," as in I haven't even looked at how it works, it's not production-ready, but it's kind of a cool prototype. The moment vibe coding mean everything that touches AI, it effectively ends up needing programming, because we're all moving in a direction where our code is mediated through AI at some point. (00:11:17): So, what do we call it for professionals? I've gone with agentic engineering, because I think the thing to emphasize is these coding agents, right? If you're asking ChatGPT to knock out some code, that's a different thing from if you're running Codex and having it write the code, debug the code, test the code, all of that. I think that agentic engineering is such a deep and fascinating discipline, because the art of getting really good results out of this, the art of having them help you build software you could deploy to a million people, that's never going to be easy, that's never going to be trivial. That's always going to require a great deal of depth of experience in how software works and how these agents work, and I love that. (00:11:58): I'm kind of writing a book about it now that I'm publishing a chapter at a time on my blog. The best form of writing, because I don't have an editor or any pressure from a publisher, is just when I feel like writing another chapter I can do that, but there's so much to discuss. But yeah, so I think right now the frontier is how do we build professional software using coding agents? How do we build software that is ... I don't just want to build software that's good, I want us to build software that is better than we were building before. If the agents let us move a bit faster, but we're still churning out the same quality of software, that's less interesting to me than if the software we're producing has less bugs, more features, it's higher quality, it's better software, because we're harnessing these tools. (00:12:41): The really interesting future is something which some people have been calling the dark factory pattern or software factories. This is the idea where right now if you're a professional using these tools, the way you do it is you tell them what to build and then you look at the code and you review that code really carefully and make sure it's doing the right thing. What does it look like if you're not reviewing the code, if you're not looking at that code, but you're also not vibe coding, you're not throwing everything to the wind and seeing what happened? You're applying professional practices and quality expectations to code that you're not directly reviewing. (00:13:15): The reason it's called the dark factory is there's this idea in factory automation that if your factory is so automated that you don't need any people there, you can turn the lights off. The machines can operate in complete darkness if you don't need people on the factory floor. What does that look like for software? This company called StrongDM has been pushing this and doing some really interesting experiments around this. That I think is the ... that's futuristic. We're trying to figure out what that looks like and how we can responsibly build software in that way right now, and making some quite interesting discoveries about things that work and things that don't work, but that to me is the next barrier.
turns.zh: 咱们说说这两类吧：一边是"氛围编程（vibe coding）"，另一边是……我很喜欢 Andrej Karpathy 对氛围编程的原始定义——就是你连代码都不看，纯粹凭感觉走。你说"给我造个能干活 X 的东西"，它造出来，你玩玩。看着不错，挺好；不太对，就来回磨。非常放手，你根本不看代码……所以他最初说"这适合图个乐、做原型"，结果后来远远超出了那个范畴。(00:09:21)：我觉得今天氛围编程实际就是——我给它下的定义是：你不看代码、不在乎代码、甚至可能看不懂代码。现在非程序员也能跟 Claude 说要造什么，它就给造个小应用，我太爱这个了。我绝对热爱这种"让电脑替你干活、用顺手小工具自动化生活琐事"的能力民主化。当然问题也随之而来：负责任地用这能力，是有上限的。我喜欢跟人说：如果你氛围编程是给自己用，bug 最多坑的是你自己，那你随便造，完全没问题。一旦你写的代码是给别人用的、你的 bug 真可能伤害到别人，那就得停下来想想：等等，这不是负责任的使用方式。(00:10:15)：难点在于，判断什么"负责任"、什么"不负责"，本身就是专家级技能。比如你一开始爬别人的网站，可能因为请求太猛把人家站点搞挂。不懂行的话，能闯的祸太多了。但我热爱这种解放感，也爱人们能带着自己敲出来的原型来开会、把想法演示出来。这些事都妙极了。(00:10:42)：一直以来的争论是：当一名专业软件工程师用这些工具写出"经过自己审阅核对、可上生产的真代码"时，这该叫什么？很多人也管它叫氛围编程。我觉得这贬低了"氛围编程"这个词，因为能说"我氛围编程搞了这玩意儿"是有用的——意思是"我连它怎么跑都没看，不是生产级，但算个酷原型"。一旦氛围编程等于"所有碰了 AI 的东西"，它就 basically 变成"需要编程"了，因为我们都在朝"代码终归要经过 AI 中转"的方向走。(00:11:17)：那专业人士的活儿叫什么？我选了"智能体工程（agentic engineering）"，因为我想强调的是那些编程智能体。你让 ChatGPT 敲段代码，跟你跑 Codex 让它写代码、调试代码、测代码，是两码事。我觉得智能体工程是一门极深极迷人的学问——想从里面拿到好结果、想让它帮你造出能部署给百万人的软件，永远不容易、永远不 trivial，永远需要对"软件怎么跑、智能体怎么跑"有极深的理解，我太爱这个了。(00:11:58)：我正在写一本这方面的书，一章一章地发在我博客上。最好的写作方式莫过于此——没有编辑、没有出版社压力，想写下一章就写。可要聊的实在太多。总之，现在的疆界是：我们怎么用编程智能体造专业软件？我不要只造"还行"的软件，我要造比从前更好的软件。如果智能体只是让我们快一点、却还是产出同样质量的软件，那不如我们借工具造出 bug 更少、功能更多、质量更高、更棒的软件来得有意思。(00:12:41)：真正有意思的未来，是有些人所谓的"黑灯工厂模式（dark factory pattern）"或"软件工厂"。想法是这样的：现在专业玩家用这些工具的方式是，你告诉它们造什么，然后你看着代码、仔细审阅、确认它干得对。可如果你不审代码、不看那些代码，但你也不是在氛围编程、不是把一切抛到脑后看运气，而是对你并不直接审阅的代码套用专业实践和品质要求，那会是什么样？(00:13:15)：叫"黑灯工厂"，源于工厂自动化的一个意象：如果工厂自动化到根本不需要人，你就可以关灯。机器在彻底黑暗里也能转，因为车间里没人也行。软件这边会是什么样？有家公司叫 StrongDM 在这条路上推得很猛，做了些真正有意思的实验。我觉得那就是……那是未来式。我们正试着想清楚它长什么样、怎么负责任地这么造软件，而且已经有了些关于"什么行、什么不行"的有趣发现，但对我而言，那是下一道关隘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's follow that thread, so what is this factory doing? So there's an element of no one's looking at the code really, but how does that change how software's built? Are people still coming up with the ideas and telling in this factory, build this thing for me?
turns.zh: 咱们顺着这条线往下：这个"工厂"到底在干什么？所以这里面有"其实没人看代码"的成分，但它怎么改变了软件的构建方式？人们还在出点子、告诉这个工厂"给我造这个"吗？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Oh, exactly.
turns.zh: 哦，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: So, this is the fascinating thing is ... so there's a policy of nobody writes any code and quite a few companies are beginning to introduce that now, because-
turns.zh: 所以有趣的地方在于……现在有些公司开始推行"谁都不写代码"的政策，因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to be clear, the policy is you cannot write code, it has to be written by AI.
turns.zh: 说清楚点，这政策就是：你不能写代码，必须由 AI 来写。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: You can type code into a computer, exactly.
turns.zh: 你能把代码打进电脑，对，就是那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Honestly, six months ago I thought that was crazy, and today probably 95% of the code that I produce I didn't type it myself. So that world is practical already, because the latest models are good enough that you can tell them, "Oh no, rename that variable and refactor that and add this line there," and they'll just do it and it's faster than you typing on the keyboard yourself. (00:14:47): The next rule though is nobody reads the code, and this is the thing which StrongDM started doing back in, I think it was August last year. They said, "Okay, we're not going to read the code." So, what does that mean? How do you produce software that works and is good if you're not reading the code? They've come up with a whole bunch of answers. One of the most interesting was the way they did testing where in traditional software some companies will have a QA department. The engineers write about your software and then you throw it over the wall to the QA department and they test it furiously to figure out if it's working or not. (00:15:21): That I think went out of fashion a bit over the past five to 10 years from what I've seen in Silicon Valley, because you kind of want your engineers to take responsibility for the code they're writing being good. But what if you can simulate that QA department? So, what StrongDM were doing is they had a swarm of agent testers who were actually simulating end users. So, the software that they were building ... this is crazy. The software is security software for access management, so when you start as a company and somebody needs to assign you access to Jira and then give you access to Slack and all of that kind of thing, they were building software for that. (00:15:59): That's very security-adjacent. That's not the kind of thing that you should be vibe coding at all based on most people's understanding of how the world works. They're a legitimate security company who've been doing this stuff without AI for years, so it's not like they didn't understand the risks. So, the way they did their testing is they had this swarm of simulated employees all in a simulated Slack channel saying things like, "Hey, could somebody give me access to Jira?" The Slack channel itself is simulated, we'll talk about that in a moment, and 24 hours a day they're making requests and saying, " Hey, I need access to Jira," and all of those kinds of things at an enormous cost. They were spending $10,000 a day on tokens, I think, simulating with these end users.
turns.zh: 说实话，半年前我觉得这疯了，可今天我产出的代码大概 95% 都不是自己敲的。所以那个世界已经实际存在了，因为最新模型好到这种程度：你跟它们说"哎把那变量改个名、重构一下、在那儿加一行"，它们直接就做了，比你自己敲键盘还快。(00:14:47)：但下一条规矩是"没人读代码"——这是 StrongDM 大概去年八月开始干的事。他们说"好，我们不读代码了。"那意味着什么？你既不读代码，又怎么造出能跑、又好的软件？他们想出了一整套答案。最有意思的一条是关于测试：传统软件里有些公司设有 QA 部门。工程师写完软件，往墙那边一扔给 QA 部门，他们拼命测，看它跑不跑得起来。(00:15:21)：据我在硅谷的观察，这做法过去五到十年有点过时了，因为你更希望工程师对自己写的代码质量负责。但如果你能模拟出那个 QA 部门呢？StrongDM 的做法是搞了一群"智能体测试员"，真实模拟终端用户。他们造的软件……这太疯了。那是做访问管理的安软，就是公司里新人入职，得给他分配 Jira 权限、再给 Slack 权限之类，他们就在造这种软件。(00:15:59)：这跟安全高度相关，按大多数人的常识，这根本不是该"氛围编程"的东西。他们是正经安全公司，没 AI 那会儿就干这行多年，所以绝非不懂风险。他们的测试方式是：搞一群模拟员工，全在一个模拟的 Slack 频道里说"嘿，谁能给我开个 Jira 权限？"——这 Slack 频道本身也是模拟的，待会儿聊——这些"人"一天 24 小时不停提需求："嘿我要 Jira 权限"等等，成本惊人。我记得他们一天在 token 上就花了一万美元，用这些终端用户做模拟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A day?
turns.zh: 一天？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: I believe so, but it meant that the software was being very robustly tested in all of these different ways. Yeah, it's kind of similar to having a manual QA team, except one that never sleeps. I thought that was fascinating as a example of thinking outside of the box. Taking this question, how do we tell our software's good if we're not reviewing the code and trying to find creative answers to it. (00:17:02): The other thing that was interesting is that the Slack channel itself wasn't actually Slack, because it turns out if you test against real software like Slack and so forth, they all have rate limits and they won't let you just run 10,000 simulated people at a time. So, what they did is they built their own simulation of Slack and Jira and Okta and all of this software they were integrating with. The way they did that is they basically took the API documentation for the public APIs for Slack and the open source client libraries, and they told their coding agents, "Build this. Build me a simulation of this API," and they did. (00:17:38): So, this company is ... and this is one of the things ... I went to a demo that they gave back in October. One of the things that really sat with me is that they had their own simulated version of Slack and Jira and all of these different systems that they could then build their software against, which cost them nothing, because once they spun it up it was a little Go binary that sat there, and they even had interfaces. They had a fake version of the Slack interface that they'd vibe coded up that let them see what was going on. Absolutely fascinating.
turns.zh: 我相信是，但这也意味着软件在接受各种方式极其扎实的测试。有点像有个不睡觉的手工 QA 团队，我觉得这作为"跳出框框思考"的例子太妙了——拿"如果不审代码，我们怎么知道软件好"这个问题，去想些创意答案。(00:17:02)：另一件有趣的事是，那 Slack 频道其实不是真 Slack，因为一旦拿真 Slack 之类的软件测，它们都有速率限制，根本不让你同时跑一万个模拟人。所以他们自己造了 Slack、Jira、Okta 以及所有要集成的软件的模拟版。做法是：基本上把 Slack 公开 API 的文档和开源客户端库拿过来，告诉编程智能体"照这个造，给我造个这 API 的模拟"，它们就造出来了。(00:17:38)：这家公司……我在十月去看了他们的演示，最让我记挂的一点就是：他们有自己的模拟版 Slack、Jira 和那一整套系统，可以拿真对着造软件，而且零成本——因为一旦跑起来，就是个小小的 Go 二进制文件搁在那儿，他们甚至做了界面。有个他们氛围编程出来的假 Slack 界面，能让人看清发生了什么。绝对迷人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a cool story, and I love these stories of just companies at the bleeding edge trying to see what's possible and have an advantage essentially. So, what I'm hearing here is the QA piece is like the new piece in this factory. So we already have Codex, Claude Code, they can go off and build stuff. Is the innovation here, okay, now you've built all this stuff, is it actually any good? Is there a reason why Codex and Claude Code couldn't do this themselves? Why do you need this factory concept?
turns.zh: 这故事太酷了，我就爱这种"站在最前沿探边界、借此抢到优势"的公司故事。所以我听到的是：QA 这块是这个工厂里"新"的拼图。我们已经有 Codex、Claude Code 能跑出去造东西了。这里的创新点是——好，你造了一堆东西，它到底行不行？为什么 Codex 和 Claude Code 自己不能干这个？你为什么需要"工厂"这个概念？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: I think they can. You can tell Claude Code, fire up a subagent that uses Playwright to simulate a browser and all of that kind of thing. You'd have trouble getting it to run 24 hours a day. I mean, maybe it would work. But certainly I think what's interesting to me isn't so much the software you're using. It is these big ideas, these techniques that you're using to try and answer these questions, because even if your QA team, your virtual QA team says this is good, doesn't mean it's secure, right? It doesn't mean that you've got all of those other characteristics that you care about. (00:19:04): At the same time, the agents are getting really good at security penetration testing now. This is a new thing ... I think, again, in the past three to six months they've started being credible as security researchers, which is sending shockwaves through the security research industry. They were like, "Wow, we didn't think that they'd get to this point." What's interesting there is both OpenAI and Anthropic have specialist security models that they will not release to the general public, because they can be used to break into websites. So they have invite only registered security researchers can apply for access, and they've been producing vulnerability reports against popular open source software. (00:19:47): I think Firefox just a few days ago, maybe last week, said that they'd done a release, which was assisted by Anthropic. Anthropic had discovered 100 potential vulnerabilities in Firefox and responsibly reported them to Mozilla who then fixed them. That's an interesting one as well, because we're seeing a lot of this in the wild and it's just incredibly frustrating for maintainers, because there are these people who don't know what they're doing who are asking ChatGPT to find a security hole and then reporting it to the maintainer. The report looks good. ChatGPT can produce a very well-formatted report of the vulnerability. It's a total waste of time, it's not actually verified as being a real problem. The difference with Anthropic and Firefox is that Anthropic's security team actually did do the work. They didn't report whatever the agent said, they actually verified that it was a good quality report before they handed it over.
turns.zh: 我觉得它们能。你可以让 Claude Code 拉起一个用 Playwright 模拟浏览器之类的子智能体。难点是让它一天 24 小时连轴转，也许能行吧。但对我而言有趣的，倒不是你用的软件，而是你用来回答这些问题的那些大思路、那些技法，因为就算你的虚拟 QA 团队说"这没问题"，也不代表它安全，对吧？不代表它具备你在乎的其他那些特性。(00:19:04)：与此同时，智能体现在做安全渗透测试已经相当厉害了。这是新动向……我想也就过去三到六个月，它们作为安全研究员开始靠谱了，正在安全研究圈引发地震。那些人惊呼："哇，没想到它们能到这一步。"有意思的是，OpenAI 和 Anthropic 都有专门的安全模型，不对公众发布，因为能被用来攻破网站。他们搞了邀请制，注册安全研究员可以申请，然后拿这些模型对热门开源软件产出漏洞报告。(00:19:47)：我记得 Firefox 几天前、大概上周说发了个版本，是 Anthropic 协助的。Anthropic 在 Firefox 里发现了 100 个潜在漏洞，负责任地报给 Mozilla，对方修掉了。这件事也很有意思，因为我们在现实里看到太多这类事，对维护者来说简直 frustrate 透顶：有些人不懂行，让 ChatGPT 找个安全洞，然后报给维护者。报告看着挺像样——ChatGPT 能产出格式极其规范漂亮的漏洞报告——但纯属浪费时间，因为它压根没验证过这是真问题。Anthropic 和 Firefox 那次的差别在于：Anthropic 的安全团队是真的下了功夫，不是把智能体说的原样甩出去，而是真验证过这是份高质量的报告，才交出去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's going to be a lot to talk about on the security side. You've done a lot of thinking and writing about the dangers there, but I want to follow this thread. So, in terms of what AI's been doing for teams. If you think about it, it's kind of going on the middle and expanding, so it's taking on more and more of the building components. It's doing code reviews now with QA, as you've been describing, constantly building, and it feels like the front of that is the big now gap in opportunity, which is coming up with the idea. What the heck should we build? 'Cause then once you tell the AI, build this thing, as you're describing, it's getting better and better at building something great. Have you had any luck yet with using AI there? And do you think it starts to eat that and just becomes the strategy PM basically?
turns.zh: 安全这块要聊的还多。你对那边的风险想了很多、写了很多，但我想顺着这条线走。就 AI 对团队在做的事而言，它有点像从中间往外扩，接管了越来越多的构建环节。现在它连 QA 带代码审查都在做，正如你描述的那样不停在造。而前方那个最大的机会缺口，似乎就是"想出点子"——我们到底该造什么？因为一旦你告诉 AI"造这个"，正如你说的，它造出好东西的能力越来越强。你在这方面有摸到门道吗？你觉得它会蚕食这块、基本变成"战略 PM"吗？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: So, one of the most interesting problems we're having with all of this is we've taken the writing code bit and we've massively accelerated that, now the bottlenecks are everywhere else, right? How do we redesign our processes? Now that the bit that used to take the longest, it used to be you'd come up with a spec and you handed it to your engineering team, and three weeks later, if you're lucky, they'd come back with an implementation for you to then start. Now maybe that takes three hours, depending on how well-established the coding agents are for that kind of thing. So, now what, right? Now, where else are the bottlenecks? (00:21:59): I mean, there's coming up with the initial ideas. Anyone who's done any product work knows that your initial ideas are always wrong. What matters is proving them, it's testing them. We can test things so much faster now, because we can build workable prototypes so much quicker. So there's an interesting thing I've been doing in my own work where any feature that I want to design, I'll often prototype three different ways it could work, 'cause that takes very little time, and then I can start experimenting them and trying them and seeing which ones I like. That feels to me like the really transformational step here is that when you get AI involved in your ideation phase, it's much more about the prototypes. It's about, okay, we can see a UI prototype is free. Now, ChatGPT and Claude will just build you a very convincing UI for anything that you describe, and that's how you should be working. I think anyone who's doing product design isn't vibe coding little prototypes is missing out on the most powerful boost that we get in that step. (00:23:02): But then what do you do, right? Given your three options now that you have instead of one option, how do you prove to yourself which one of those is the best? I don't have a confident answer to that. I expect this is where the good old-fashioned usability testing comes in. Get somebody on Zoom, screen shared using your software, see what happens. You can tell the AI to do it and you can simulate your users with the AI. I don't think that's credible. I don't think you're going to get as good results from ChatGPT pretending to click around on your prototype than you would from an actual human being.
turns.zh: 我们眼前最有趣的问题之一是：写代码这块被我们大幅加速了，现在瓶颈跑到别处了，对吧？我们怎么重新设计流程？以前最耗时的环节是：你想个 spec，交给工程团队，运气好三周后他们带回一个实现让你开工。现在也许三小时就搞定，取决于那类编程智能体有多成熟。所以现在呢，对吧？别的瓶颈在哪？(00:21:59)：比如想出最初的点子。做过产品的人都知道，你最初的点子永远都是错的，关键在验证、在测试。我们现在能快太多地去测，因为能快太多地造出能用的原型。我自己工作里有个很有意思的玩法：任何我想设计的功能，我常会用三种不同做法各做个原型——因为花不了多少时间——然后开始试、开始挑，看我喜欢哪个。对我来说，真正的变革性一步是：当你把 AI 拉进"构思（ideation）"阶段，重点就更多落在原型上。就是说，OK，UI 原型免费了、随手就有。现在 ChatGPT 和 Claude 会直接给你造出任何你描述东西的、极具说服力的 UI，你就该这么干。我觉得做产品设计的，要是还没在氛围编程小原型，就是错过了这一步里我们拿到的最强助力。(00:23:02)：可然后你怎么办，对吧？现在你有三个选项而不是一个，你怎么向自己证明哪个最好？我没有特别有把握的答案。我猜这里就该老派可用性测试上场了：拉个人上 Zoom，屏幕共享用你的软件，看发生什么。你可以让 AI 做、也可以用 AI 模拟用户，我觉得那不靠谱。ChatGPT 假装在你的原型上乱点，得到的成果，比不上真人对着的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. A question I've been tackling is just where are human brains going to continue to be valuable? What I'm hearing here is there's the initial idea. You made such a good point here. It's like the initial idea's often not the actual winning idea, it's just the beginning of an idea. So there's the idea for the feature, then there's the try it out, prototype it, help you narrow on the direction, build it, make it awesome, get it out into the world. It feels to me like AI's going to be really good at suggesting ideas and coming up with initial ideas, and I wonder if the human brain ... it's not like maybe someday we don't need human brains at all, and that's a whole other discussion, but maybe the next phase is AI will help us come up with great ideas.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。我一直在琢磨的一个问题是：人脑到底在哪些地方还会持续有价值？我听到的是——有最初的点子。你这点说得真好：最初的点子往往不是真能赢的那个，它只是个起点。所以先是功能点子，然后试、做原型、帮你收窄方向、造出来、做到惊艳、推向世界。我感觉 AI 会非常擅长"建议点子、出最初的点子"，而我在想人脑……也许有一天我们根本不需要人脑了——那是另一个话题——但下一阶段也许是 AI 帮我们想出好点子。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: I mean, that's been the case for probably a couple of years now, they've been strong enough to do really good brainstorming. I like to compare it to the thing where when you've got a group brainstorming exercise, you book a meeting room for an hour, you've got a whiteboard, you get a dozen people in, and the first two-thirds of that brainstorming session, honestly it's kind of just everyone going through the most obvious basic ideas, right? You get them all out on the whiteboard, you get them all up, and then things get interesting when you start saying, "Okay, well, let's talk about these, let's start combining them." (00:24:45): The AI is so good at that first two-thirds of the ideas. I brainstorm with them all the time where I just get them to spit out all of the obvious stuff, and they'll come up with 20 things and they'll all be kind of dumb, they just won't be very interesting. What gets interesting is when if you ask them for 20 more and now-
turns.zh: 这个嘛，大概已经两三年了，它们强到真能做很棒的头脑风暴。我常拿它跟这种场景比：你搞一场集体头脑风暴，订间会议室一小时，白板一立，拉十来个人进来，前三分之二基本就是大家把最显而易见的初级点子过一遍，对吧？全列上白板，然后有意思的才来——你开始说"好，咱们聊聊这些，开始组合它们"。(00:24:45)：AI 在那前三分之三里强得离谱。我整天跟它们头脑风暴，让它们把明显的东西全吐出来，能蹦出 20 个，全都挺蠢、没啥意思。有意思的是当你让它"再来 20 个"，到那份清单末尾，开始出现"不算好点子、但指向有趣方向"的东西。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: What gets interesting is when if you ask them for 20 more and now by the end of that list, you're beginning to get things which are not good ideas, but they point you in interesting directions. There are so many other tricks like this. You can tell AI to combine weird fields. You can say, "Okay, I want ideas for marketing my new SaaS platform inspired by marine biology," and you see what happens. And most of it will be complete junk, but there might be a spark that gets you to the good idea. So I love them as brainstorming companions on that front.
turns.zh: 有意思的地方在于，当你让它"再来 20 个"，到那份清单末尾，开始出现那些"不算好点子、却把你引向有趣方向"的东西。这类小技巧太多了。你可以让 AI 组合冷门领域，比如"给我点子，用海洋生物学的灵感来营销我的新 SaaS 平台"，看会怎样。大多纯垃圾，但也许有一星火花能把你引向好点子。所以我超爱把它们当头脑风暴搭档。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me of a chat I had with David Placek. He's a expert naming person. He helps companies come up with names for product. And one of the things that he does at his company is he creates three teams to come to brainstorm names. So for example, let's say Windsurf was a product they named. So the first team is, "Okay, this is an AI IDE thing." That's exactly what it is. Second team is, "Okay, this is a boat. You're naming a boat and here's the constraints. And then here, this is a spaceship. So name it from that perspective." And he finds the best names come from those other directions where it's a different metaphor with the same sort of benefits. (00:26:10): Okay. So what I'm hearing here is this is good. This is good for humans right now, that there's still opportunity for us to contribute to the process.
turns.zh: 这让我想起跟 David Placek 的一次聊天。他是起名专家，帮公司给产品起名。他公司里的做法，是组三支队伍来头脑风暴起名。比如 Windsurf 是他们起的产品名。第一队："OK，这是个 AI IDE 工具。"就它本来的样子。第二队："OK，这是条船，你在给一条船起名，约束如下。"第三队："这是艘 spaceship，从那个视角起名。"他发现最好的名字来自那些"换了隐喻、但好处类似"的其他方向。(00:26:10)：所以我的意思是，这东西现在对人是有益的——我们在这个过程中还有贡献的机会。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: And actually, I want to stand in defense of software engineers for a bit because on the one hand, these things can write code. That used to be our thing. I'm finding that using coding agents well is taking every inch of my 25 years of experience as a software engineer, and it is mentally exhausting. This is something which people are talking a lot more about now. I can fire up four agents in parallel and have them work on four different problems, and by 11:00 AM, I am wiped out for the day, because there is a limit on human cognition in how much, even if you're not reviewing everything you're doing, just how much you can hold in your head at one time. (00:26:57): And it's very easy to pop that stack at the moment. There's a sort of personal skill that we have to learn, which is finding our new limits. What is a responsible way for us to not burn out and for us to use the time that we have? And I've talked to a lot of people who are losing sleep because they're like, "My agents could be doing work for me. I'm just going to stay up an extra half hour and set off a bunch of extra things and I'm waking up at 4:00 in the morning." That's obviously unsustainable. I hope that that's a novelty thing. The agents only really got good in the past four to five months. We're all learning what that looks like and what that lets us do. But it's concerning. There's an element of gambling and addiction to how we're using some of these tools. (00:27:39): But to stand in defense of software engineers, I get great results out of these things because they are amplifiers of existing skills and experience. And I have 25 years of existing pre-AI experience, which I can now amplify because I can talk to the agent at a very high level. I can use sophisticated engineering language that I've mastered over the years, which they appear to know as well, and we can collaborate incredibly effectively. And it means I can look at a problem and I can say, "This problem is a one-sentence prompt and I know it'll find that bug and fix that bug," as opposed to this other problem, which is who knows how big a problem. (00:28:18): There is a flip side to this, which is that I've got 25 years of experience in how long it takes to build something, and that's all completely gone. That doesn't work anymore because I can look at a problem and say, "Okay, well, this is going to take two weeks. It's not worth it." And now it's like, yeah, but maybe it's going to take 20 minutes, because the reason it would've taken two weeks was all of the crufty coding things that the AI is now covering for us. And that I've been finding really interesting and challenging. (00:28:44): I constantly throw tasks at AI that I don't think it'll be able to do, because every now and then it does it. And when it doesn't do it, you learn. You learn, okay, Opus 4.6 still can't do this particular thing, but when it does do something, especially something that the previous models couldn't do, that's actually cutting edge AI research. You can be the first person in the world to spot that AI can now do X just because you were the person you found it couldn't do it and you've been keeping that sort of backlog of interesting tasks for it.
turns.zh: 其实我想替软件工程师说几句公道话，因为一方面这些玩意儿能写代码，那曾是我们的活儿。我发现要把编程智能体用好，得把我 25 年软件工程经验每一寸都使上，而且精神透支。现在大家聊这个多了。我能同时拉起四个智能体攻四个不同问题，到上午 11 点我就瘫了——因为哪怕你不全审阅，人脑一次能装下的东西也有上限。(00:26:57)：此刻很容易"爆栈（pop the stack）"。我们有门得学着掌握的个人技能，就是找到自己的新极限：怎么负责任地不 burnout、怎么用好手头的时间？我聊过很多人，他们失眠，因为"我的智能体还能替我干活，我就再熬半小时、多派一堆活儿，结果凌晨四点惊醒"。那显然不可持续。我希望那只是新鲜劲儿。智能体也就是过去四到五个月才真变好，我们都在学它长啥样、能让我们干啥。但挺让人担心的。用这些工具里，有点赌博和上瘾的味道。(00:27:39)：不过替工程师说公道话：我从里面拿到好结果，是因为它们是既有技能和经验的放大器。我有 25 年"前 AI"经验，现在能放大——因为我可以用很高层的语言跟智能体对话，用我这些年掌握的老练工程术语，它们好像也懂，于是我们配合极有效率。这意味着我看一个问题能说"这问题是句话的 prompt，我知道它能找到并修掉那个 bug"，而另一个问题则是"谁知道多大个坑"。(00:28:18)：反过来说，我对"造一样东西要多久"有 25 年经验，而这全作废了。因为以前我看问题会说"好，这得两周，不值当"；现在变成"嗯，但也许只要 20 分钟"——因为原本要两周，是因为里头那些脏活累活现在 AI 替我们扛了。这点我发现既有趣又挑战。(00:28:44)：我 constant 地把我觉得 AI 干不了的任务砸给它，因为偶尔它真能干成。干不成，你就学到：哦，Opus 4.6 还干不了这个，但干成了、尤其是前代干不了的事，那其实是最前沿的 AI 研究。你能成为世界上第一个发现"AI 现在能干 X"的人，就因为你一直记着它干不了、还给它攒着那堆有趣任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such an interesting line of discussion, this idea that let's say 10X engineers, to use that phrase, are going to be more valuable is what you're describing here because you can work with these tools much more effectively. What do you think of junior engineers? Just what's happening there? What's their future?
turns.zh: 这段讨论太有意思了——你说的其实是：所谓 10 倍工程师，会因为这些工具而更有价值，因为他们能跟工具配合得更高效。那你怎么看初级工程师？他们那边在发生什么？未来如何？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: So Thoughtworks, the big IT consultancy, did an offsite about a month ago and they got a whole bunch of engineering VPs in from different companies to talk about this stuff. And one of the interesting theories they came up with is they think this stuff is really good for experienced engineers. It amplifies their skills. That's great. It's really good for new engineers because it solves so many of those onboarding problems. If you talk to Cloudflare and Shopify both said they were hiring a thousand interns over the course of 2025 because the intern onboarding costs, it used to be takes a month before your intern can do anything useful. Now they're doing something useful within a week because the AI assistant helps them get up and running faster. (00:30:14): The problem is the people in the middle. If you're mid-career, if you haven't made it to super senior engineer yet, but you're not new either, that's the group which ThoughtWorks resolved were probably in the most trouble right now. That's the open question because they don't have that expertise to amplify and use with these tools and it's not as benefit... They've got all of the boosts that the beginners were getting, they've got already, so that's an interesting open question right now for me is it's more the sort of mid-level as opposed to the beginners or the advanced people.
turns.zh: Thoughtworks 那家大型 IT 咨询公司，大概一个月前搞了场 offsite，请了一堆不同公司的工程 VP 来聊这个。他们提出的一个有趣理论是：这东西对经验丰富的工程师极好，放大了他们的技能，棒。对新人工程师也极好，因为它解决了那么多入职（onboarding）难题。跟 Cloudflare 和 Shopify 聊，俩家都说 2025 年招了一千名实习生，因为实习生入职成本以前要一个月才能干点有用的事，现在一周内就能上手——全靠 AI 助手帮他们更快跑起来。(00:30:14)：问题是中间那批人。如果你职业生涯中段、还没到超级资深、但也不是新人，那 Thoughtworks 判定为眼下最危险的一群。这是个开放问题，因为他们既没有那种能被放大、拿来用的深厚专长，而新人得到的那些助力他们早就有。所以对我来说，有意思的开放问题是：受冲击更大的，是中间层，而不是新手或高阶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting how AI is coming at the middle of so many things. It's coming at the middle of the product development process. It's coming at the middle of seniority. There's probably other examples. And I'm guessing this is true for all functions, like PMs designers too, just new PMs designers, maybe because being AI native basically is what you're describing and ramping up much more quickly. (00:31:09): I guess while we're on this topic, a lot of listeners here are just like those people in the middle. What would your advice be to them to help them avoid becoming a part of the permanent underglass?
turns.zh: 太有意思了，AI 正从中间切入这么多东西。它从产品开发流程的中间切入，从资历的中间切入，估计还有其他例子。我猜所有职能都这样——PM、设计师也是，只是新 PM、新设计师，也许因为"AI 原生"基本就是你说的那样，上手快得多。(00:31:09)：既然聊到这，很多听众就是那些"中间的人"。你对他们有什么建议，帮他们别沦为"永久被玻璃罩住（underglass）"的那批？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: That's a big responsibility you're putting on me there. I think the way forward is to lean into this stuff and figure out how do I help this make me better? A lot of people worry about skill atrophy. If the AI is doing it for you, you're not learning anything. I think if you're worried about that, you push back at it. You have to be mindful about how you're applying the technology and think, "Okay, I've been given this thing that can answer any question and often gets it right, doesn't always get it right. How can I use this to amplify my own skills, to learn new things, to take on much more ambitious projects?" (00:32:01): Something I've been enjoying, I think the thing I've enjoyed most about this as a software engineer is that my level of ambition has shot right up because now, I never used Apple Script because Apple Script is a whole programming language you have to learn. And I've been using Apple Script for like two and a half years now because ChatGPT knows Apple Script and so now I can automate things on my Mac and that's great. And previously, the fact that it would take me two or three months to learn basic Apple Script was enough for me never to use it. And now I've got all of these technologies that I'm using because that two to three month initial learning curve has been shaved right down. (00:32:37): I think that applies to everything else. I'm getting much better at cooking. I've been using Claude, it turns out, excellent chef, which doesn't make sense because it doesn't have taste buds, but it can give you the global average of the world's guacamole recipes, which turns out is good guacamole. So that's been really interesting, like trying to apply this stuff just for sort of self-improvement. I think that's a really useful skill to have because honestly, everything is changing so fast right now. The only universal skill is being able to roll with the changes. That's the thing that we all need. (00:33:11): Weirdly, the term that comes up most in these conversations about how you can be great with AI is agency. People, human beings have agency and we use that agency to decide what problems to take on and where to go. I think agents have no agency at all. I would argue that the one thing AI can never have is agency because it doesn't have human motivations. Sure, you can tell it, "Make more money," or whatever, but it's never going to be able to decide on what makes sense for it to act on next. So I'd say that's the thing is to invest in your own agency and invest in how do I use this technology to get better at what I do and to do new things.
turns.zh: 你这可是把大责任压我身上了。我觉得出路是拥抱这东西，想清楚"它怎么让我变得更好"。很多人担心技能萎缩（skill atrophy）：AI 替你干了，你啥也没学到。我觉得你要是担心，就反推它。你得清醒地看待怎么用这技术，想"OK，我被给了个能回答任何问题、常常对、不总对的东西。我怎么用它放大自己的技能、学新东西、接更雄心勃勃的项目？"(00:32:01)：有件事我玩得特开心——作为一个软件工程师，我最享受的是我的野心水平直线上升，因为现在，我以前从不用 AppleScript，因为它门得学整套编程语言。结果我现在用 AppleScript 都用两年半了，因为 ChatGPT 懂 AppleScript，于是我能在 Mac 上自动化做事，爽。以前"得花两三个月学基础 AppleScript"这点，就够让我永远不碰它。现在一堆技术我都在用，因为那两三个月的入门曲线被削平了。(00:32:37)：我觉得这适用于一切。我做菜也进步飞快。我用 Claude，发现它是个极棒的厨子——虽然没道理，因为它没味蕾——但它能给你全世界牛油果酱食谱的"全球平均值"，而这居然是好吃的牛油果酱。所以这类事，把技术用在自我提升上，挺有意思。我觉得这是项极有用的技能，因为老实说一切变得太快，唯一通用的技能就是"能跟着变"。那是我们所有人都需要的东西。(00:33:11)：很怪，这些"怎么用 AI 变得厉害"的对话里，出现最多的词是"能动性（agency）"。人是有能动性的，我们用它决定接什么题、往哪走。我觉得智能体根本没有任何能动性。我会说 AI 永远不可能有能动性，因为它没有人的动机。当然你可以让它"多赚钱"什么的，但它永远没法决定"下一步什么对它来说说得通"。所以我的建议是：投资你自己的能动性，投资"我怎么用这技术把本职做得更好、去做新事"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also to your point, be ambitious. Think big.
turns.zh: 还有一点呼应你说的——要有野心，想大一点。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's an interview with Jensen that just came out yesterday where people asked him about layoffs. There's all these layoffs happening. Is AI actually taking jobs? And he's like the reason a lot of these companies are letting people go is they don't have enough creativity or ambition for what they can do with all of these resources there, because they're not letting people go. They have so much they want to do. And obviously easier said than done and it's not always the case, but I think that's an interesting way of approaching. And now that we have this power, people almost underestimate what they can do with it and don't fully lean into it. So I love this advice of just try to be a little more ambitious, try to stuff that you think is impossible and see it might be actually possible.
turns.zh: 昨天刚出了个采访 Jensen（黄仁勋）的节目，有人问他裁员的事。现在到处都在裁员。AI 真在抢工作吗？他的意思是，很多公司之所以让人走，是因为面对这么多资源，他们没足够的创造力或野心去干那些能干的活——因为他们没在裁员，他们有太多想做的事。当然说起来容易做起来难，也不总是这样，但我觉得这是个有意思的切入角度。既然我们有了这股力量，人们几乎低估了自己能用它做成什么、也没完全扑上去用。所以我特别喜欢这个建议：试着更敢想一点，去碰那些你以为不可能的事，看看它可能其实做得到。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: My New Year's resolution this year was the opposite. Every previous year, I've always told myself this year, "I'm going to focus more. I'm going to take on less things." This year, my ambition was take on more stuff and be more ambitious. We've got these tools. Bring it all in. Let's try and do everything. I don't know if that was a good New Year's resolution, but that's what I went with.
turns.zh: 我今年的新年决心正好相反。往年每年我都跟自己说，今年"我要更聚焦、少接些事"。今年我的志向反而是多接活、更敢想敢干。我们有这些工具了，全招呼上，啥都试试。我不确定这是不是个好决心，但我就是这么定的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So how's it going so far? How do you feel about this decision?
turns.zh: 那目前进展如何？你自己对这决定感觉怎么样？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: It's fun. I'm enjoying myself. I think I'll probably get to the end of the year and I'll be like, "Wow, the most important things that I should have been focusing on did not get done," but that's the case when it is my ambition to do them.
turns.zh: 挺好玩的，我很享受。我大概会到年底的时候才意识到："哇，那些我最该专注的要事，一件都没做完。"——不过就算当初我把它们列成志向，结果也一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a converge, diverge sort of situation. Next year could be refocused.
turns.zh: 这是个先发散、再收敛的过程。明年可以重新聚焦。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Absolutely. Yeah.
turns.zh: 那当然。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. Kind of along those lines, I want to come back to this point you made about how you're working harder and you're fried early in the day. This is such an interesting, I don't know, contradiction almost. AI is supposed to make us more productive. It's supposed to give us more time off. It's supposed to let us sit around and watch Netflix and create wealth and productivity in the world. It feels like the people that are most AI-filled are working harder than they've ever worked. There's this anxiety described of, "My agents aren't running. I got to stay on top of them." What do you think is going on there? Is this just, like you said, maybe it's a temporary novelty thing and then we'll be like, "All right, I don't need to be this productive"? Is there anything else there?
turns.zh: 哎呀。顺着这条线，我想回到你提过的那个点——你怎么现在干得更狠、一大早就累瘫了。这简直是个矛盾。AI 本该让我们更高效、本该给我们更多休息时间、本该让咱们瘫着刷 Netflix、顺便创造财富和生产力。可感觉那些最沉迷 AI 的人，反而比以往任何时候都更拼命。还有一种焦虑，叫"我的智能体没在跑，我得盯着它们"。你觉得这是怎么回事？就像你说的，可能只是新鲜劲儿、过后我们就"行吧，不必这么拼"？还是另有别的原因？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: I really hope it's a novelty thing. And I am actually getting much more... I'm getting more time, but I'm exhausted.
turns.zh: 我真希望那只是新鲜劲儿。而且我确实……我其实时间变多了，但我累瘫了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like your brain is exhausted?
turns.zh: 你是说脑子累瘫了？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: My brain is exhausted. I've got more time to go and do things and I do things and it's great, but the exhaustion from that sort of intensity of work has been a really big surprise for me. That's been something which I've been observing, especially since November as all of this stuff started ramping up. And yeah, I think that the concern there comes down... It's always expectations from other people. If you work for a company that's expecting you to get five times more done, that's going to be exhausting. And maybe we'll see. And I think the good companies with good management are paying attention to this and that they don't want to burn out their best employees for the short-term gain, but lose people over it. But yeah, it's a big tension. I think those of us on the sort of leading edge of the AI boom are feeling it first. I imagine it's going to come for everyone else as well.
turns.zh: 我脑子累瘫了。我有了更多时间可以出去干点事，我也干了，挺好，但这种高强度工作带来的疲惫，对我是个挺大的意外。这事儿我一直在观察，尤其从十一月这股浪潮起来之后。我觉得这里的隐患说到底……永远是"别人的期望"。如果你所在的公司指望你产出翻五倍，那肯定累。也许往后看就明白了。我觉得管理到位的好公司会注意到这点，它们不愿为了短期收益烧掉最优秀的员工、最后把人弄丢。但总之这是个巨大的张力。我们这些站在 AI 热潮最前沿的人先感受到了，我猜迟早也会落到其他人头上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other element of this though that we haven't mentioned is, and you've mentioned a couple times, it's actually really fun. The drive here is not-
turns.zh: 不过我们还没提到的另一面是——你也提过好几次——这事其实特别好玩。这里的驱动力并不是——

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: I'm enjoying myself so much. Absolutely. It's so fun. A lot of my friends have been talking about how they have this backlog of side projects. For the last 10, 15 years, they've got projects they never quite finished and ideas they thought would be cool. And some of them are like, "Well, I've done them all now. Last couple of months I just went through and every evening I'm like, 'Let's take that project and finish it and that one and that one and that one and that one.'" And they almost feel a sort of sense of loss at the end where they're like, "Well, okay, my backlog's gone. Now what am I going to build?"
turns.zh: 我太享受了。绝对是。太好玩了。我很多朋友都在聊他们那堆"积压的副业项目"。过去十到十五年，他们总有些没真正做完的项目、一些当时觉得挺酷的点子。现在有些人说"我全做完了。过去几个月我每天晚上就挨个把那些项目捡起来做完"。到头来他们甚至有点失落感："好吧，积压清空了，那我接下来造什么？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it comes back to that factory. I was talking to the founder of Linear the other day and this idea of the factory, and we were just like, a factory doesn't sound like a place that'll create amazing products. It feels like what are the chances that it'll create something beautiful and innovative? So either that's the wrong word or it's just this will lead to bad stuff probably.
turns.zh: 对，这又绕回那个"工厂"了。前几天我跟 Linear 的创始人聊，聊到"工厂"这个点子。我们就想，工厂听起来不像个能造出惊艳产品的地方。它造出漂亮、有创新东西的概率有多大？所以要么这词用错了，要么这路子大概率会造出烂东西。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: I feel like the word artisanal does... Artisanal handcrafted software I think is going to be valued more. Something I've noticed in my own work is sometimes I'll have an idea for a piece of software, Python library or whatever, and I can knock it out in an hour and get to a point where it's got documentation and tests and all of those things and it looks like the kind of software that previously I've spent several weeks on, and I can stick it up on GitHub and everything, and yet I don't believe in it. And the reason I don't believe in it is that I've got to rush through all of those things. I think the quality is probably good, but I haven't spent enough time with it to feel confident in that quality. (00:38:21): Most importantly, I haven't used it yet. It turns out when I'm using somebody else's software, the thing I care most about is I want them to have used it for months. I want other people to have put that software into practice. So I've got some very cool software that I've built that I've never used. It was quicker to build it than to actually try and use it. And so the way I've been dealing with that is I always put alpha on it. If you see my software and it says it's an alpha, that probably means I haven't actually used it yet for most of my project, which is a bit of a cheat code, alpha [inaudible 00:38:53]. But isn't that interesting? It used to be if you looked at software and it had high quality tests and documentation and everything, it meant it was good, and now that signal is gone.
turns.zh: 我觉得"匠人（artisanal）"这个词更贴切……"匠人手作软件"我估计会更值钱。我自己工作里注意到一件事：有时我冒出个点子，要写个软件、Python 库什么的，我能一小时搞定，还带文档、带测试、样样齐全，看起来就像我以前得花好几周才能做出来的那种软件。我能把它丢上 GitHub 等等，可我自己却不信它。我不信的原因是，我全是赶着把那些事一口气冲完的。质量估计还行，但我没花够时间跟它相处，所以没底气说它质量好。(00:38:21)：最要命的是，我还没用过它。结果发现，我用别人软件时最看重的，是希望人家已经用了好几个月、希望有其他人真把它用在了实践中。所以我有好些很酷、自己却从没用过的软件——造它比真正去用它还快。我的应对办法是：一律给它标个 alpha。如果你看到我的软件标着 alpha，那大概意味着我其实还没真正用过它——大部分项目都这样，算个取巧的法子吧，alpha [听不清 00:38:53]。但你不觉得这很有意思吗？以前你看一个软件，有高质量测试、有文档、样样齐全，那就代表它好；现在这个信号没了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's almost like we need a proof of work for this versus the blockchain.
turns.zh: 这简直像我们需要一个"工作量证明（proof of work）"，对应区块链那种。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: A proof of usage.
turns.zh: 一个"使用量证明"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Proof of use.
turns.zh: 使用证明。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. On this note of handcrafted code, I don't know if you know this, this is so interesting, data labeling companies are buying old GitHub repos of handwritten code to train their models on, and they're paying a lot of money for artisanal human written code.
turns.zh: 哎呀。说到手作代码，不知道你知不知道——这太有意思了——数据标注公司正在收购老 GitHub 上"手写代码"的仓库来训练模型，而且为这些"匠人级人类手写代码"出价不菲。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Oh, that's fascinating. That's the pre-World War II, the metal that you can dig up from old shipwrecks, which is before the first nuclear explosions, and so it's not got the radiation baked into the metal. It's that whole thing.
turns.zh: 哦，那太神了。这不就是"二战前金属"那回事嘛——从老沉船里打捞上来的、第一颗核弹爆炸之前的金属，没被辐射腌入味。就是那个梗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. That's a great metaphor.
turns.zh: 哇。这比喻绝了。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: That's fascinating.
turns.zh: 太神了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So they're looking for code pre-2022, I think, whenever ChatGPT emerged.
turns.zh: 对。所以他们找的是 2022 年之前、也就是 ChatGPT 冒头之前的代码。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if you've got some, you can make a fortune.
turns.zh: 所以你要是手头有，能发笔横财。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Problem is, I open source all my stuff, so it's already out there. It's been used to train the models already.
turns.zh: 问题是，我把自己的东西全开源了，所以早就在外面了。已经被用来训过模型了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's been slurped up already.
turns.zh: 早就被"吸"走了。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. Okay. Let me ask you this question. I'm just curious about this prediction. I know you're not a prediction person, although you do make predictions and you seem to be right often. When do you think 50% of engineers in the world will be... AI will be writing 100% of their code? How close to that do you think we are?
turns.zh: 哎呀。好，那我问你这个。我对你那个预测挺好奇。我知道你不是爱预测的人，不过你确实做预测，而且好像常常说对。你觉得世界上 50% 的工程师，会在什么时候变成 100% 的代码都由 AI 写？你觉得我们离那一步还有多近？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: So I'm going to refactor that to 95% of their code. I don't think we'll get to it. But yeah, it's very difficult to say worldwide, partly because there are cultural differences. I spend way too much time on hack and use, and something I've noticed about hack and use is a conversation that starts at midnight Pacific time and goes until 8:00 AM, very different tone because it's the Europeans. And the Europeans are a lot more AI skeptic than the Americans are generally. So I think different countries are going to have different cultures around this. (00:40:54): At the same time, I think it's become undeniable this year that this stuff produces good code. It used to be that you could say, "I don't use this stuff because the code is bad." And that was a justifiable position. That's not justifiable anymore. The code is now good. It's good code, for my definition of good code at least. So we're saying 50% of engineers, let's say 15 engineers, majority of their code, it could happen by the end of this year. It could, because the technology is good enough now. (00:41:26): And I feel like the challenge now is getting people to learn how to use this stuff, which is difficult because using this stuff, everyone's like, "Oh, it must be easy. It's just a chatbot." It's not easy. That's one of the great misconceptions in AI is that using these tools effectively is easy. It takes a lot of practice and it takes a lot of trying things that didn't work and trying things that did work. But yeah, I expect by the end of this year, it will not be uncommon to have an engineer say that almost all of that code is written by AI.
turns.zh: 那我把问题改一下，改成"95% 的代码"。我觉得到 100% 不太可能。不过话说回来，全球范围真的很难说，部分因为文化差异。我在 Hacker News 上泡太久了，注意到一个现象：一场从太平洋时间午夜聊到早上八点的讨论，调性会完全不同，因为那是欧洲人在线。欧洲人普遍比美国人更怀疑 AI。所以我觉得不同国家会发展出不同的文化。(00:40:54)：但与此同时，今年有一点已经无可否认了：这东西就是能产出好代码。以前你可以说"我不用这玩意儿，因为代码太烂"，那是个站得住的立场。现在站不住了。代码现在就是好，至少按我对"好代码"的定义是这样。所以你说 50% 的工程师、比如 15 个工程师、大部分代码由 AI 写，这到今年年底就可能发生。真可能，因为技术现在已经够好了。(00:41:26)：而我现在觉得最大的挑战，是让人学会怎么用这东西——这很难，因为大家都觉得"哦，肯定很简单，不就是个聊天机器人嘛"。才不简单。AI 最大的误解之一，就是以为"有效使用这些工具"很容易。它需要大量练习，需要大量试错、试那些行得通和不行的事。不过我预期到今年年底，一个有工程师说"我几乎全部代码都是 AI 写的"将不再稀奇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was the same rough idea I had. And how crazy is that, how quickly-
turns.zh: 这跟我的粗略判断一样。而且你想想多疯狂、变化多快——

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: It's wild.
turns.zh: 太野了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... this job has changed and what is possible. And I think people, this is a good example of people underestimate how quickly things can change. I think Dario was predicting this a year or two ago, just, "Oh, 100% of code's going to be written by AI," and we were just like-
turns.zh: ……这个工作已经变了，可能性也变了。我觉得这正好说明人们低估了变化能有多快。我记得 Dario（Anthropic 的 Dario Amodei）一两年前就预言"哦，100% 的代码都会由 AI 写"，我们当时就——

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: We all laughed at him. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我们都笑话他来着。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Exactly. Like, "What are you talking about? It's so bad. It's so bad at writing code." And this might come for other jobs that people don't see coming, which is scary and interesting and exciting.
turns.zh: 对，正是。就像"你在说什么呢？这玩意儿烂透了，写代码烂得要命。"而这可能会降临到别人没料到的其他工作上，这既吓人、又有趣、又让人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Honestly, I'm not an AI doomer in the slightest. The economics of it do make me nervous. Are we really going to wipe out a tenth of white collar knowledge work jobs in the next few years? I really hope not, because I don't know how the economy adapts to that. So yeah, that's complicated.
turns.zh: 老实说，我一点都不是 AI 末日论者。但这背后的经济学让我不安。我们真要在未来几年里抹掉十分之一的白领知识工作岗位吗？我真心希望别这样，因为我不知道经济怎么适应。所以，这很复杂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Actually, I'm doing a report that's coming out, it'll come out ahead of this episode, looking at the job market in tech. And surprisingly, just at tech companies, we're at the highest number of open engineering roles, open PM roles.
turns.zh: 对。其实我正在写一份会在这集之前发布的报告，看科技行业的就业市场。有意思的是，单看科技公司，现在开放的对工和 PM 岗位数是最高的。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Except for during the crazy peak during COVID. So it's kind of coming back to that. Basically, it's the highest number of open roles in three and a half-ish years for engineers and PMs at tech companies globally.
turns.zh: 除了新冠期间那波疯狂峰值。所以基本是回到了那个水平。大致说，这是三半年左右以来，全球科技公司里对工程师和 PM 开放岗位数最高的时候。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: That's very interesting. It's funny, isn't it? Because you get all of these headline grabbing-
turns.zh: 太有意思了。很讽刺，是不是？因为你看到那一堆抢眼的大标题——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Layoffs.
turns.zh: 裁员。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Yeah. Was it Block that laid off 4,000 people recently?
turns.zh: 对。最近裁了 4000 人的是 Block 吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。对。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: But the question there is always how much of that is AI and how much of it is overhiring during COVID and re-corrections and all of that kind of thing? It's always very difficult to tell. So the number of open jobs, on the one hand, maybe that's a better signal, but on the other hand, the recruitment market has been driven completely crazy by all of this stuff. All of the job ads are written by AI, the resumes are AI. People in recruitment are saying that it's never been this hard to filter through and hire people, and people who are hiring jobs say they applied to 200 things and got nobody hearing back. So it's hard, right? The macroeconomic indicators for this stuff are lagging. And at some point we should start getting more confident numbers about what the impact actually is.
turns.zh: 但问题永远是：这里面有多少是 AI 的锅，又有多少是新冠期间过度招聘、然后回调之类的？一直很难分清。所以开放岗位数，一方面也许是个更好的信号，但另一方面，招聘市场已经被这股浪潮彻底搞疯了。所有招聘广告是 AI 写的，简历也是 AI 写的。招聘的人说，筛人和招人从没这么难，而找工作的人说投了 200 份石沉大海。所以很难判断，对吧？这方面的宏观指标是滞后的。迟早我们该拿到更靠谱的数字，看清实际影响到底多大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Interestingly, the number of recruiter open roles is also approaching record numbers-
turns.zh: 对。有意思的是，招聘人员本身的开放岗位数也在逼近历史高位——

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Hilarious. That's so interesting.
turns.zh: 笑死。太有意思了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... which is an interesting leading indicator of demand for hiring. So there's interesting trends in spite of the layoffs. So yeah, what a wild world. So you've mentioned this book you're working on. This is the agentic engineering pattern stuff, right?
turns.zh: ……这其实是个有趣的"招聘需求"领先指标。所以尽管在裁员，趋势却挺有意思。哎呀，这世界真疯狂。你提过你在写的那本书，就是"智能体工程模式"那套，对吧？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So I want to talk about this. So you point it out. People think it's easy to build with AI. It's like, "Oh, it's going to do all these things for us. What are we going to do all day?" To your point, it's actually not. There's a lot of very specific skills you need to do this well, and you're putting them together on your blog. We'll point to it. I want to talk through a few of them to help people do this better. So one is this idea of just writing code is cheap now. You touched on this a bit. Maybe just share why this is such an important thing to know and keep in mind.
turns.zh: 好，酷。那我想聊聊这个。你点出来了：人们以为用 AI 造东西很容易，好像"哦，它全帮我们干了，我们白天干啥去？"——但正如你说的，其实并不容易。要把它用好，需要很多很具体的技能，而你正在博客上把它们串起来。我们会给出链接。我想挑几个聊聊，帮大家做得更好。第一个就是"写代码现在很便宜"这个点。你前面提过一点。聊聊为什么这是件特别重要、要牢记的事。

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: So I think this is the single biggest shock in all of this. The reason that we have to rethink how we build, how we work as software engineers is that the thing that used to take the time takes way less time. It's never been the case that programmers spend 90% of their typing code into a computer. There's so much additional work around that, but it still used to be... People talk about how important it is not to interrupt your coders. Your coders need to have solid two to four hour blocks of uninterrupted work so they can spin up their mental model and churn out the code. That's changed completely. My programming work, I need two minutes every now and then to prompt my agent about what to do next, and then I can do the other stuff and I can go back. I'm much more interruptable than I used to be. (00:45:45): But yeah, so the thing that used to take the time is now the thing that takes way, way less time. What does that mean for everything else that we do? And that doesn't just affect programmers. It affects entire teams around software development. But as an individual programmer, you have to start thinking, okay, I can churn out 10,000 lines of code now in the time that it would take me to write 100. How do I make that code good? How do I make sure that I'm not just churning out total slop that adds up to technical debt that slows me down? How do I take the fact that code is now cheap and use that to produce better code? Because I don't just want cheap code. I want really good code that does what I need it to do that I can extend in the future that's got all of those characteristics of code that's useful and can be used in production.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是整件事里最大的一个冲击。我们之所以要重新思考"怎么构建、软件工程师怎么工作"，就是因为那个曾经最耗时的环节，现在耗时少太多了。程序员从来也不是把 90% 时间花在往电脑里敲代码上——周围那一大堆附加工作才是，但以前仍然是……大家总说别打断写代码的人，他们需要整块两到四小时不受打扰，才能建立起心智模型、把代码吐出来。这点彻底变了。我现在做编程，隔一阵子只用花两分钟给智能体下个"下一步干啥"的指令，然后就能去干别的，回头再看。我比以前容易被打断了。(00:45:45)：但总之，那个曾经耗时的东西，现在耗时少太多了。这对我们做的其他一切意味着什么？这不只影响程序员，它影响软件开发周围整个团队。但作为个体程序员，你得开始想：好，我现在能在过去写 100 行的时间里吐出 1 万行代码。我怎么让这些代码是好代码？怎么确保我不是在吐一堆最终变成技术债、拖慢自己的垃圾？我怎么利用"代码现在很便宜"这件事，去产出更好的代码？因为我要的不只是便宜的代码。我要真正好的代码——能按我的需求干活、未来能扩展、具备那些"有用、能上生产"的代码该有的全部特质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The point you made earlier I think is a really important one along these lines, which is when you start a project, you fire off three different versions of it and that helps you pick a direction. And that's only possible because code is so cheap now, right?
turns.zh: 你前面提的那点，我觉得顺着这条线特别重要：就是项目一开始，你同时甩出三个不同版本，帮你定方向。而那之所以可能，正是因为现在代码太便宜了，对吧？

turns.speaker: Simon Willison
turns.en: Right. Prototyping is almost free, I think. And that really impacts me because throughout my entire career, my superpower has been prototyping. I've been very quick at knocking out working prototypes of things. I'm the person who can show up at a meeting and say, "Look, here's how it could work." And that was kind of my unique selling point, and that's gone how anyone can do what I could do. But you still have to learn when it's appropriate to prototype, how to think about prototyping, how to get the tools to build useful prototypes that you can use to explore things.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得原型几乎免费了。这点对我冲击很大，因为我整个职业生涯的"超能力"就是做原型。我一向能很快敲出能跑的东西。我是那种能开会时甩出"喏，看，这东西能这么运转"的人。那曾是我的独特卖点，而现在谁都能干我以前能干的事。但你还是得学会：什么时候该做原型、怎么思考原型、怎么让工具造出能用来探索的有用原型。
